It's interesting that he brings up Diablo 2 and Diablo 3 (and Quake for that matter), though, because I think it really foregrounds why these discussions are so fraught.

I worked in early AAA in the late 90s, and it's true that games were often quite rough around the edges. But they were also often biting off WAY more than they could chew, inventing genres and innovating like crazy, often in messy ways that didn't always work. But that meant players were often also routinely and genuinely surprised by the experiences they encountered in even big budget games.

He lists a bunch of quality of life and balance issues that were fixed in Diablo 3 compared to Diablo 2... but, well, Diablo 2 was obviously _important_ in ways that Diablo 3 wasn't. It's a much greater game.

And lurking in the background is the hard fact that often the progress with software (certainly game software) entailed turning to much better software engineering standards, using much better external libraries or game engines with much larger teams, and relying on much more process to capture and filter all those rough edges... and along the way, you've built a much, much larger team with a much larger burn rate, and so all those experiments and innovations become much more dangerous and need to be corralled and controlled and mostly stifled, and as the cost of all this to build skyrockets your entire game design _has_ to focus on your business model and your microtransaction story and your live services first and foremost, because you've boxed yourself into a corner where that cash flow issue is the central fact of your game / software design.

(I experienced this evolution first hand in the FPS space)

All of which is to say, I think there are multiple different axes at play here for evaluation, and it's probably fair to say that software _undefinably_ was much worse in the past along some of them... but not all of them. And there are probably deep tensions and tradeoffs between some of those axes.

I think this entirely discussion really is muddied, though, too, by the fact that hardware got radically better over this entire arc as well, and so many programming techniques in the past that made software more brittle or crash prone hinged on memory and computation optimizations techniques that really had nothing to do with the software culture of then or now. It was just a response to the realities of the hardware.

Also, aside from the dupe bugs, his "improvements" in Diablo 3 I consider it's downside. Changes that are framed as QoL changes in games are very frequently just reductions in risk or investments in your character.

His general outlook seems to be that the small teams of the past creates more rough edges and that the larger teams on modern AAA games creates a smoother experience but requires more concern for income because the cost is so much higher for the larger team.

I get that comparison but I think he's totally missed the advantages of the small team. The cheaper dev cost means less risk of financial ruin if the game fails which means innovations are less risky. Less developers means the vision of one person can shine through more which results in a more creative end-result, for better or worse.

The "too many cooks" in the kitchen is a real problem of modern software, especially games. Huge budgets mean games need huge audiences to be successful which means everyone needs to like it. The death of productivity software is, unsurprisingly, anything that stands in the way of productivity. The save bugs he mentions are real killers. But for games, as an art form, the turn from focusing on the vision of the artist to the desires of the audience makes for uninspiring work.

I'll take bugs all day long if it comes with a unique experience.

There are real QoL changes that simply make the game better - but there are also QoL changes that simply remove the game. It's an extremely delicate balance, and easy to get wrong in ways you don't notice until it's too late.

For example, quest tracking in modern games is phenomenal, and people used to add addons to do that - but there's really a way in which "figure it out yourself" and/or read the guidebook/talk to people was better. Same with pug tooling - no need to find a group anymore, the computer does that for you, but you also don't develop relationships with those around you.

There are limits. USB keyboards are just always going to be slower than PS/2 keyboards. You can close the gap, but USB is just fundamentally adding wrapping layers that introduce latency over the direct polling PS/2 used. And there's a lot of this at the hardware level, where standardized connections with complex protocols replace weird custom connectors. USB is most definitely easier to plug something in to than PS/2 ports, where you had different ports for mouse and keyboard and they weren't interchangeable. (Ok, some very late motherboards supported using either in a single port, but it wasn't the way most PCs worked.)

You can do a lot at the high levels, but everything needs to be reworked from the hardware level up to match the latency of older systems.

> USB is just fundamentally adding wrapping layers that introduce latency over the direct polling PS/2 used

PS/2 did not use polling, it was entirely event-driven. On keypress, the keyboard sent a serial message to the 8042 controller [1], which then raised the appropriate interrupt line on the CPU, which caused the keyboard ISR [2] to be executed. The serial clock was a bit flexible, but usually sat around 10-16 kHz [3], and so the 11-bit serial message took at most 1 ms to send.

It is USB that uses polling. The keyboard describes itself using endpoint descriptors, and after obtaining these, the host controller periodically polls it with an IN token, to which the keyboard responds with its state changes since the last poll [4]. The earliest USB keyboards preferred fairly slow polling rates, but modern keyboards can be polled every 1 ms [5]. If directly connected to a motherboard USB port, a modern USB keyboard will have pre-software input latency on par with a PS/2 keyboard.

[1]: https://wiki.osdev.org/I8042_PS/2_Controller

[2]: https://wiki.osdev.org/Interrupt_Service_Routines

[3]: https://retrocomputing.stackexchange.com/q/15607/25565

[4]: https://threeboard.dev/documentation/threeboard/how_usb_keyb...

[5]: https://www.usb.org/sites/default/files/hid1_11.pdf pp. 68-69

IMO it's a bit more nuanced than what the author portrays it as. Broadly, software used to be much worse on the micro-level but better on the macro-level i.e. architecture.

Since it was much harder to make stuff, you really had to architect it well or otherwise it would simply fall apart. For example in assembler you need discipline in your calling conventions, layout and so on, otherwise it just corrupted, you needed to follow sensible naming conventions otherwise it degenerated into unreadable label spaghetti and so on.

Nowadays it's the other way around, the micro level is so much better due to libraries, code reuse, LLMs and better languages/tools, you can use highly sophisticated data structures and functions at your fingertips. In exchange, you can afford to skimp on architecture because computers are fast anyway, and the programming languages don't let you make a huge mess. (Most don't have unstructured goto/jumps, can't corrupt memory accidentally, etc.)

However, this has the cost of making larger programs a nightmare to maintain and systems suffering from a "death of thousand cuts" i.e. on the micro level all is well but when you look at the entire system it's a sprawling unreliable mess. This is where rewrites often happen ;)
Architecture is still important for large systems. And there are tons of legacy systems with spaghetti code.

I think one look at video games throughout history should probably shoot down the idea that software is uniquely bad nowadays compared to how it was in the past. The Atari era had enough poorly made games that the industry basically crashed in North America, and its revival in the 8-bit era didn't really change as much as expected. The fact the internet is full of YouTube reviewers akin to the Angry Video Game Nerd should be evidence that incredibly bad, often blatantly non functional software was a common occurrence throughout history.

There were games released in a pre-alpha state (Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing), games that were basically released in a normal alpha state (Superman 64, Action52, etc) and there were games which literally didn't work because of major programming issues (SQIJ! had a player character which couldn't move due to the game only looking for lower case inputs while leaving the caps lock on).

And that's only the most extreme examples. Plenty of games had broken features and mechanics, or were outright impossible to complete due to poor level design and a lack of proper testing. Fan games, mods, ROM hacks and indie game scenes from the earlier days were just as notorious for works that were barely functional.

Generally games are at least now functional nowadays, with even the worst tending not to outright crash to a black screen or leave you with a player character that's completely unable to move. In many ways, the baseline level of competence arguably seems to be getting higher, with the march of AI meaning the worst is probably better than it might have been previously been.

Outside of games, it's worth noting how deeply insecure and flawed many older websites and programs were. There was a time where storing passwords in plain text was more of a norm, where input validation and sanitisation was often forgotten about, and where sites getting hacked was just as common an occurrence as today. Many Perl devs probably recoil in horror after hearing the term "Matt's Script Archive".

Are some things worse? Sure, performance seems to have become increasingly ignored in recent years, with web page sizes getting incredibly bloated and latency going through the roof. In some places there's more bad software overall, since the ability to vibe code it means non-programmers are building software more than ever. And some big companies that used to be respectable have let standards slip a lot (see Epic Games, Microsoft, etc).

Sturgeon's Law/Revelation held back then, and still holds today: 90% of everything is crap.
